title: Zermatt or Chamonix for skiing: which is better?
author: Matt
intro: Zermatt and Chamonix are two of the most famous ski towns in the Alps, one under the Matterhorn and one under Mont Blanc. Zermatt is higher, more reliable for snow, car-free and pricier. Chamonix is a lively French town with some of the most dramatic, challenging skiing anywhere, and it's much quicker to reach from Geneva. Here's how to choose.
seo_title: Zermatt or Chamonix for skiing? How they compare
seo_description: Zermatt is higher, snow-sure and car-free but pricier; Chamonix is closer to Geneva, cheaper and more challenging. Snow, cost and transfers compared.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **More reliable snow:** Zermatt
- **Quicker transfer:** Chamonix
- **Expert and off-piste:** Chamonix
- **Lower prices:** Chamonix, usually

Both are bucket-list ski trips with famous mountain views. Pick Zermatt for high, snow-sure cruising with the Matterhorn above you, a car-free village and skiing over to Italy. Pick Chamonix for steep, adventurous skiing, a real town with lively bars, and a short hop from Geneva.

sections.heading: Side by side
sections.text:
| | [Zermatt](/destinations/zermatt) | [Chamonix](/destinations/chamonix) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Country | Switzerland | France |
| Village height | about 1,600 m | about 1,000 m |
| Top lift | about 3,900 m | about 3,800 m |
| Transfer from Geneva | about 3½ to 4 hrs by train | about 1¼ hrs by road |
| Currency | Swiss franc | euro |
| Best for | snow-sure cruising, views | experts, off-piste, nightlife |

The heights are approximate. Chamonix's top lift is the Aiguille du Midi, which is for sightseeing and off-piste routes rather than ordinary pistes. Both are an hour ahead of the UK.

sections.heading: Zermatt
sections.text:
Zermatt is a car-free village of wooden chalets and smart hotels, with electric taxis and the Matterhorn towering over the end of the valley. Its ski area is one of the highest in the Alps, so the snow is reliable from early winter to late spring, and a glacier area is open for much of the year.

- **Skiing:** long, scenic red runs that suit confident intermediates, with lifts up to the Matterhorn Glacier Paradise.
- **Italy:** ski over the border to Cervinia for lunch, as the two areas are linked.
- **Food:** mountain restaurants are some of the best in the Alps, though prices are high.

Local knowledge: Zermatt is expensive even by Swiss standards. A lift pass, a mountain lunch and a drink in the village can cost a lot more than in France, so budget for it.

sections.heading: Chamonix
sections.text:
Chamonix is a proper year-round town at the foot of Mont Blanc, with a lively centre of bars, restaurants and shops. Its skiing is split into several separate areas along the valley, linked by buses and a train, rather than one big network.

- **Skiing:** steep, high runs that suit good and expert skiers, with areas like Brévent-Flégère and Les Grands Montets.
- **The Vallée Blanche:** a famous long off-piste glacier run from the Aiguille du Midi, which you should only do with a qualified mountain guide.
- **Nightlife:** busy après-ski bars in town, much more so than in Zermatt.

Watch out: Chamonix's lower slopes can be short of snow in a mild winter, and getting between areas takes time. It's not the easiest choice for beginners or for families with small children.

sections.heading: Getting there from the UK
sections.text:
- **Zermatt:** fly to Geneva or Zurich, then take the train, changing at Visp, which takes around three and a half to four hours from Geneva. Cars aren't allowed in the village, so you leave the car at Täsch if you drive.
- **Chamonix:** fly to Geneva, then take a shared transfer, a bus or a hire car, about an hour and a quarter. It's quick enough for a long weekend.

Geneva has direct flights from most big UK airports in winter, with easyJet, British Airways, Swiss and Jet2's ski flights. Our [best ski resorts for a weekend from the UK](/blog/best-ski-resorts-for-a-weekend-from-the-uk) post covers short transfers, and [skiing by train from London](/blog/ski-by-train-from-london) covers going without flying.

sections.heading: Which should you choose?
sections.text:
- **Choose Zermatt** for the most reliable snow, long scenic runs, a car-free village and skiing into Italy, if the budget allows.
- **Choose Chamonix** for steep and off-piste skiing, a lively town, lower prices and a quick transfer from Geneva.
- **For intermediates:** Zermatt, with its long, cruisy runs.
- **For a long weekend:** Chamonix, as the shorter transfer leaves more time on the slopes.

For a gentler mix of skiing and winter sun, see our [ski and sun holidays](/blog/ski-and-sun-holidays) post. Can't agree? Add both to somewhere.party, give everyone points to vote with, and let the draw decide.

faqs.question: Is Zermatt or Chamonix better for beginners?
faqs.answer: Zermatt is a little easier, with more gentle cruising runs, though it's expensive. Neither is ideal for complete beginners, and Chamonix's spread-out areas and steep runs suit good skiers best.

faqs.question: Which has better snow, Zermatt or Chamonix?
faqs.answer: Zermatt usually does, because its village and ski area are higher. Its glacier area means skiing is possible for much of the year.

faqs.question: How do you get from Geneva to Zermatt?
faqs.answer: By train, changing at Visp, in about three and a half to four hours. Zermatt is car-free, so drivers park at Täsch and take the shuttle train.

faqs.question: Can you ski from Zermatt to Italy?
faqs.answer: Yes. Zermatt's ski area links with Cervinia in Italy, so with the right lift pass you can ski over the border for lunch and back. Check the weather, as the high lifts close in strong winds.

faqs.question: Is Chamonix cheaper than Zermatt?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes. Lift passes, food and drink in France tend to cost less than in Switzerland, though Chamonix is still one of the pricier French resorts.
